source.title: MoHETS: Long-term Time Series Forecasting with Mixture-of-Heterogeneous-Experts
source.authors: Evandro S. Ortigossa; G. Lutsker; E. Segal

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a model-size sweep for time-series forecasting, a setting outside language-model pretraining, and describes how forecasting metrics change with size.
record.gate_note: Only the scalability analysis in Appendix B.3 is recorded. Other forecasting benchmarks and architectural ablations do not test the scaling-law versions. The paper does not fit power laws or report fitted exponents.
record.test_reason: Appendix B.3 trains MoHETS at four sizes (0.3M to 21.4M activated parameters) on four time-series datasets and reports held-out forecasting MSE/MAE against size. This is a weak, non-language test of V5. It has four points and no power-law fit, so it only shows the direction of improvement, not the functional form.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say larger MoHETS improves MSE and MAE, that this aligns with scaling laws and confirms scalability in time series, and that it shows potential for further scaling. They attribute the slight MSE rise at dmodel=384 on ETTm1/ETTm2 to overfitting on limited data.
record.recipe_differences: This is a time-series forecasting model-size sweep using MSE and MAE, not a language-model held-out cross-entropy power-law fit or compute-optimal allocation study.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported size trends differ by dataset: ETTm1 and ETTm2 MSE turn slightly upward at dmodel = 384, while Weather and ECL metrics continue to improve.
record.problems: The scalability sweep covers only dmodel values 64, 128, 256, and 384. It reports plotted MSE/MAE trends without exact values, uncertainty estimates, or power-law fits. The authors excluded ETTh1 and ETTh2 because of overfitting risk and Traffic because of hardware constraints.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant scalability results were left out; the paper reports the sweep in Figure 4 for four datasets and two metrics.

untested.parts: The power-law functional form itself (no fit, no exponents, four sizes over about 1.8 orders of magnitude). Data or compute scaling. Image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
No fixed-parameter shape comparison. The size variants confound depth and width.
No downstream prediction from scale or loss.

missing.what: Parameter counts of the four size variants (0.3M/1.3M/7.4M/21.4M activated; 0.6M/2.5M/14.5M/42.7M total), with depth and heads also varying. Rows report only dmodel.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is thin: a four-point appendix sweep, figure only, no uncertainty, and no power-law fit. Training settings per size in the sweep are not stated; the main results used different epochs and batch sizes per dataset (Table 9). The paper is not an original source. Kaplan et al. is cited only as background.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
Tests forecasting metric trends across model size in time-series data, but does not fit or test a power-law form; does not examine image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance prediction from scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices or training setups.

relationships.condition: Weather and ECL (larger datasets), 0.3M–21.4M activated parameters
relationships.reason: Both metrics are reported to fall consistently with size up to the largest model (r5–r8). This is only directional support: no power-law fit or readable values.
relationships.display_finding: Both forecasting metrics decreased consistently through the largest model, although no power-law fit was reported.

relationships.condition: ETTm1 and ETTm2 (smaller datasets), largest model
relationships.reason: MSE rises slightly from the 7.4M to the 21.4M variant, which the authors attribute to limited data. Gains bend once data becomes the bottleneck (r1, r3).
relationships.display_finding: MSE increased slightly between the 7.4M and 21.4M variants, which the authors attributed to limited data.
